title: Identifiability of Registration Data
description: Parent registration flow collects multiple PII elements (email, password, name, govt ID) that can directly identify the individual. The combination of these identifiers creates a high identifiability risk.
assumptions: Data is stored and processed in a manner that preserves individual identifiers

title: Linkability Across Registration Data Fields
description: Multiple data fields (email, name, govt ID) collected during registration can be linked together to create a comprehensive profile of the parent user, enabling cross-referencing with other data sources.
assumptions: Data fields are stored in a way that allows correlation

title: Disclosure of Sensitive Registration Data
description: Authentication Service processes highly sensitive data including password and government ID. Unauthorized disclosure could expose critical personal information to third parties.
assumptions: Inadequate access controls or data protection measures

title: Data Deception in Registration Information
description: Registration data (email, name, govt ID) can be falsified or manipulated by the parent user, potentially leading to fraudulent account creation or identity misrepresentation.
assumptions: User can provide false information during registration

title: Usurpation of Parent Identity
description: With email, password, and government ID collected, malicious actors could potentially impersonate the parent user through identity theft or credential compromise.
assumptions: Credentials or government ID could be compromised

title: Non-compliance with Privacy Regulations
description: Collection of government ID and sensitive personal data during registration may require compliance with data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA). Non-compliance could result in legal and reputational risks.
assumptions: Regulatory requirements apply to this data collection

title: Unauthorized disclosure of parent account data during storage
description: The Authentication Service (P1) stores parent account information in MongoDB (DS1). If MongoDB is not properly secured or access controls are insufficient, parent account data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties, violating the minimality principle and creating explicit data disclosure risk.
assumptions: MongoDB is accessible to unauthorized actors or has weak access controls
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without additional context on security measures

title: Data integrity compromise during parent account storage
description: Parent account data stored in MongoDB could be tampered with or corrupted if the database lacks proper integrity controls, encryption, or audit logging. This could lead to unauthorized modification of authentication credentials or account information.
assumptions: MongoDB lacks comprehensive integrity controls or encryption at rest
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without additional context on security measures

title: Direct identification of individuals from parent account data
description: Parent account information stored in MongoDB could directly identify individuals, especially if combined with other data sources. This creates identification risks if the data is accessed by unauthorized parties or if the data is not properly anonymized.
assumptions: Parent account data contains personally identifiable information that can be used to identify individuals
uncertainty_note: Assuming parent account data contains PII based on typical authentication service patterns

title: User Identifiability via JWT Token
description: The JWT token transmitted from the Authentication Service to the Parent User contains user data that could identify the individual. This creates a risk that the user's identity could be exposed to the parent user or intercepted during transmission.
assumptions: JWT contains personally identifiable information; transmission is not fully encrypted or protected
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identifiability threats in Process->ExternalEntity flows

title: Unauthorized Data Disclosure to Parent User
description: User data embedded in the JWT may be disclosed to the Parent User without proper authorization or consent. The parent user may not have legitimate access rights to this sensitive information.
assumptions: Parent User may not have proper authorization; JWT may contain more data than necessary
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for disclosure threats in Process->ExternalEntity flows

title: Linkability of User Data Across Systems
description: The JWT token containing user data could be linked to other data sources or systems, potentially creating a comprehensive profile of the user across multiple touchpoints.
assumptions: Parent User or other systems may correlate this data with other user information
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for linkability threats in Process->ExternalEntity flows

title: Linkability of child login to parent identity
description: Child user logs in using parent email and password, creating a link between the child's activities and the parent's identity. This could enable correlation of child's online behavior with parent's profile or other parent-linked activities.
assumptions: Parent email and password are transmitted and stored in a way that allows linking child activities to parent identity
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a reasonable fit for linkability threats in login flows

title: Identifiability of child through parent credentials
description: The child's login using parent credentials makes the child identifiable as a dependent of the parent. This could reveal family relationships and potentially expose the child's identity to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Parent email and password are visible or traceable in the authentication process
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a reasonable fit for identifiability threats in authentication flows

title: Disclosure of parent credentials during child login
description: Parent email and password are transmitted during child login, creating risk of credential disclosure to network attackers, eavesdroppers, or system vulnerabilities. This could lead to unauthorized access to parent's accounts.
assumptions: Credentials are transmitted in transit or stored insecurely
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a reasonable fit for disclosure threats in authentication flows

title: Usurpation of child identity by parent or third party
description: Since child uses parent credentials, there is risk that parent or third party could usurp the child's identity, perform actions on child's behalf, or access child-specific data without proper authorization.
assumptions: Parent or third party has access to parent credentials and could impersonate child
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a reasonable fit for usurpation threats in authentication flows

title: Linkability of Child Identity Across Systems
description: The JWT token and child profiles transmitted from the Authentication Service could be linked to identify the child user across different services or contexts, potentially enabling cross-service tracking and profiling.
assumptions: The JWT and profile data contain unique identifiers that can be correlated across systems.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a general linkability node; specific child profile context may warrant more granular analysis.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Child Profile Data
description: Child profile information transmitted via the authentication flow could be disclosed to unauthorized parties during transmission or at the receiving endpoint, violating child privacy protections.
assumptions: The transmission channel or receiving endpoint may lack adequate access controls.
uncertainty_note: Severity elevated due to child data sensitivity; actual risk depends on encryption and endpoint security.

title: Authentication Token Misuse for Identity Usurpation
description: The JWT token could be intercepted or misused by unauthorized actors to impersonate the child user, gaining access to services or data under the child's identity.
assumptions: JWT tokens may be transmitted or stored insecurely, or the token validation mechanism may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a general usurpation node; specific token validation mechanisms would refine this assessment.

title: Child Profile Identification via Government ID
description: The child's government ID is a unique identifier that can directly identify the child. When combined with name, DOB, and gender, this creates a highly identifiable profile that could be used to single out the child in various contexts.
assumptions: The government ID is stored and potentially accessible within the system

title: Profile Linking Across Datasets
description: The child's profile data (name, DOB, gender, govt ID) contains quasi-identifiers and a unique identifier that could be used to link this profile to other datasets (e.g., school records, medical records, parental data), creating a comprehensive profile of the child.
assumptions: Other datasets containing overlapping attributes exist and could be accessed or matched
uncertainty_note: Depends on external data availability and matching capabilities

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Sensitive Government ID
description: The child's government ID is highly sensitive personal data. If the Child Profile Management process is compromised or accessed without authorization, this could lead to unauthorized disclosure of the child's identity and associated sensitive information.
assumptions: The process has access to the government ID and it is stored in a potentially vulnerable manner

title: Third-Party Disclosure of Child Profile Data
description: The Child Profile Management process may share or transmit the child's profile data (including government ID) to third parties (e.g., government agencies, service providers), creating risk of unauthorized disclosure to entities beyond the intended recipients.
assumptions: The process has mechanisms to share data with external parties
uncertainty_note: Depends on system architecture and data sharing policies

title: Inference of Child's Identity and Characteristics
description: The combination of name, DOB, gender, and government ID allows for detailed understanding of the child's identity, age, and demographic characteristics. This could enable profiling and inference of additional sensitive information about the child.
assumptions: The data is accessible and can be analyzed for profiling purposes

title: Unauthorized access to child profile data during storage
description: Child profile data stored in MongoDB collection DS2 may be accessed by unauthorized parties if access controls are not properly implemented. This represents an explicit data disclosure where personal data is transferred to an unintended recipient.
assumptions: MongoDB collection has insufficient access controls or authentication mechanisms
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without additional security hardening

title: Child profile data may be identifiable
description: Child profile data inherently contains personally identifiable information (PII) that can identify the child. Even with anonymization attempts, re-identification risks exist through data correlation or metadata.
assumptions: Child profiles contain names, dates of birth, or other identifiers
uncertainty_note: Assuming child profiles contain standard PII fields

title: Child profile data integrity compromised during storage
description: Child profile data may be tampered with or corrupted during the store/update process, leading to inaccurate records that could affect parental rights, medical decisions, or legal matters.
assumptions: No adequate integrity checks or audit logging in place
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard database without additional integrity mechanisms

title: Child profile data may be linked with other datasets
description: Child profile data stored in DS2 may be linked with other data sources (e.g., medical records, school records, parental data) creating a comprehensive profile that exceeds the minimality principle.
assumptions: Data may be shared or correlated with external systems
uncertainty_note: Assuming potential for data correlation across systems

title: Unauthorized person may update child profile data
description: An unauthorized individual may impersonate a parent/guardian to update child profile information, leading to incorrect or malicious modifications of sensitive child data.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may not properly verify parent/guardian identity
uncertainty_note: Assuming authentication may not be robust enough

title: Linkability of User Search and Interaction Patterns
description: Child User's video search queries, likes, and comments can be linked across sessions to build a detailed profile of interests and preferences, potentially revealing sensitive personal information about the user's tastes, concerns, or activities.
assumptions: System logs and stores all user interactions with timestamps and user identifiers

title: Identifiability from User Comments and Interactions
description: User comments and interaction patterns on videos may contain personally identifiable information or unique behavioral signatures that could identify the user to other system users or external observers.
assumptions: Comments are publicly visible and may contain personal details

title: Disclosure of Personal Data in User Comments
description: Personal information inadvertently shared in user comments (e.g., location, contact details, personal opinions) may be exposed to other users or third parties through the video management service.

title: Improper Personal Data Management of User-Generated Content
description: Video Management Service may fail to properly manage, retain, or delete user comments and interaction data in compliance with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA), leading to unauthorized data retention or processing.
assumptions: System may not have adequate data governance policies for user-generated content
uncertainty_note: Context [5] mentions Nc.2 for improper personal data management, which applies to user-generated content like comments

title: Unintended Child Search/Watch History Disclosure
description: Child search and watch history stored in MongoDB could be disclosed to unauthorized parties or third parties, violating the minimality principle. This includes both explicit disclosure (e.g., data shared with partners) and implicit disclosure (e.g., metadata revealing search patterns).
assumptions: Data is accessible beyond intended scope; third parties may access stored history
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as it represents data disclosure across boundaries; context suggests this applies to Process->DataStore flows

title: Child Identifiability from Search/Watch Patterns
description: Search and watch history can be used to identify specific children and infer sensitive information about their interests, preferences, and behaviors. Even without direct identifiers, the pattern data could enable re-identification when combined with other data sources.
assumptions: Search/watch patterns are unique enough to identify individuals; data may be combined with other datasets
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 represents identifiability at source/flow/destination; child data is inherently sensitive

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance for Children's Data
description: Storing children's search and watch history may violate COPPA, GDPR-K, or other child privacy regulations if data collection, storage, or sharing is not strictly necessary and properly consented. Children's data requires heightened protection.
assumptions: Regulations require strict minimality and consent for children's data; current implementation may not meet these requirements
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 represents non-compliance at process level; specific regulatory requirements may vary by jurisdiction

title: Child Profile Data Integrity Compromise
description: MongoDB childprofiles collection could be tampered with, leading to corrupted search and watch history. This could result in incorrect child profiles, misleading analytics, or unauthorized modification of stored data.
assumptions: DataStore is accessible to unauthorized actors; no adequate integrity controls exist
uncertainty_note: D.1.1 represents data integrity at DataStore; assumes MongoDB has potential vulnerability to tampering

title: Improper personal data management during video upload
description: Parent User (EE1) uploading video data may result in improper personal data management, including inadequate consent management, retention policy violations, or failure to properly categorize video data as personal data under applicable regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA).
assumptions: Video data contains personal information; approval/rejection process involves regulatory compliance requirements

assumptions: Video data is sensitive personal data; P2 processes data without adequate access controls
uncertainty_note: D.1 tree node chosen based on standard disclosure threat patterns - exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Linkability of video data across systems

title: Video data linkability to other personal data
description: The video stream could be linked to other personal data about the child user (e.g., health records, location data, behavioral patterns) creating a comprehensive profile.

This disclosure may violate minimality principle if the data is not strictly required for the AI's recommendation function. Child data requires heightened protection under regulations like COPPA/GDPR-K.

description: Child browsing data may contain identifiable information (e.g., timestamps, device IDs, content preferences) that could be used to identify the child, especially when combined with other data sources. This is particularly sensitive given the age of the data subjects.
uncertainty_note: Assuming browsing data contains potentially identifiable elements

title: Regulatory Non-compliance for Child Data Processing
description: Processing child browsing data for AI recommendations may violate child-specific data protection regulations (COPPA, GDPR-K, etc.) if proper consent mechanisms, parental controls, or data minimization are not implemented. The planned nature of this flow suggests potential compliance gaps.

description: AI Recommendation Engine may derive or infer additional personal information from child browsing data (e.g., interests, behaviors, preferences) that is not explicitly collected but becomes disclosed through AI processing outputs or model training. This implicit disclosure may be avoidable.
